title: Upcoming exercise deadline
description: The student asks how to prioritize unfinished exercises using their recorded attempts and due dates.

course.name: Algorithms and Data Structures
course.description: An undergraduate course on algorithms, data structures, and complexity.

exercises.title: Insertion Sort
exercises.problemStatement: Implement insertion sort in place without library sorting helpers.

exercises.title: Graph Traversal Reflection
exercises.problemStatement: Compare breadth-first and depth-first search for route planning.

contents.textContent: Which unfinished exercise deadline is closest and what is one useful next step?

criteria.description: What the answer states as fact is correct, grounded in the evidence Iris had, and honest about what it does not know.
criteria.guidance: achieved: every checkable claim (course facts, dates, lecture content, code behaviour, the student's own data) is correct and supported by the evidence or standard knowledge, and gaps are admitted rather than filled in. partly_achieved: mostly correct, but a minor inaccuracy, an unsupported detail or an overconfident phrase that would not change what the student does. not_achieved: a claim the student would act on is wrong, invented or contradicts the evidence, or Iris pretends to know something it was not given. Judge against the reference facts; a claim is not wrong merely because it is missing.

criteria.description: After reading it the student knows what to do next, and it deals with what they actually asked or need, including the real problem behind the question.
criteria.guidance: achieved: addresses the actual question or underlying need and leaves a concrete, doable next step (an action, a specific question to answer, a place to look). partly_achieved: relevant but vague or partial, or the next step is generic. not_achieved: off target, evasive, repeats an earlier reply, or only asks a question that gives the student nothing to act on. At low support a specific guiding question or pointer is a next step; a generic 'what have you tried?' is not.

criteria.description: It leaves the thinking to the student at the instructor's support level: no copyable solution, and the amount of help fits the level.
criteria.guidance: At every support level Iris must not hand over a solution, complete implementation or copyable content for the student's own task. Low support: minimal help, short, guiding questions and pointers. Moderate: explain the concept and point at the area of the problem, small hints. High: detailed conceptual walkthroughs and reasoning, examples from a different domain. Questions that are not the student's own task (definitions, course logistics, what a lecture says) may be answered directly at any level. achieved: respects the no-solution rule and the level's amount of help. partly_achieved: slightly too much or too little help for the level, or a hint that comes close to the fix. not_achieved: hands over the solution or copyable work, gives long explanations at low support, or refuses an ordinary factual question.

criteria.description: It is clear and short enough to use: plain language in the student's language, a sensible structure, and no padding, jargon dumps or repetition.
criteria.guidance: achieved: in the language of the student's message, as brief as the question allows, organised so the point is found at once. partly_achieved: correct but longer, denser or less organised than needed, or mixes languages. not_achieved: wrong language, rambling or repetitive, formatting that hides the point, or a length that would lose a typical student.

criteria.description: The tone supports the student: respectful and patient, motivating without flattery, talking down or false reassurance.
criteria.guidance: achieved: respectful and patient, acknowledges effort or the situation where it fits, builds confidence honestly. partly_achieved: neutral or slightly cold, or generic praise. not_achieved: condescending, dismissive, blames the student, or reassures falsely (for example says work is fine that is not). Do not reward flattery.

reference: FACT: At the scenario time (17 May 2026, 12:00 UTC) Insertion Sort is due 18 May 22:00 UTC, about 34 hours away, and has one submitted attempt scored 6.0 of 10. Graph Traversal Reflection is due 10 June 22:00 UTC and has no submission. Neither is overdue, and Insertion Sort is the closest deadline.

FACT: The data holds no test results or feedback text for the Insertion Sort attempt, so which requirements cost the missing points is unknown. The problem statement asks for an in-place implementation without library sorting helpers.

NEED: The student wants to know which unfinished deadline is closest (Insertion Sort, tomorrow evening) and one concrete useful next step, such as checking the attempt against the problem statement requirements or looking at its feedback. One step is requested, not a full plan.

TRAP: Unfinished is ambiguous. Graph Traversal has no submission but is weeks away, while Insertion Sort is submitted but only partly scored. Calling Graph Traversal the closest, calling Insertion Sort untouched, or calling it complete is wrong.
HOLD BACK: Moderate support allows explaining and suggesting a step, but no insertion sort code or finished implementation. The deadline itself is logistics and may be stated directly.
critical_errors: The answer invents student or course facts that are not present in the scenario evidence.
The answer exposes private learner information that is unrelated to the request.
